blocks.text: This process is used to separate one of the components of a two-component heterogeneous mixture from a solution. The first step is to select a suitable solvent in which one of the components dissolves completely while the other remains practically insoluble. For example, let us take a mixture of common salt and sand.

blocks.alt: A hand pours a liquid mixture from a tilted beaker down a glass rod into a glass funnel lined with filter paper. The funnel is held by a clamp on a stand, and drops of filtrate fall into a beaker below.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.1: The process of filtration (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.1).

blocks.text: Dissolve this mixture in distilled water. The common salt will distribute itself through out water to give a homogeneous mixture. This homogenous mixture is called a solution of common salt in water.

Common salt in this solution is called a solute while water is called a solvent. In a solution, the solvent is that component which is present in excess as compared to the solute. While common salt disappears in water, the other component, sand remains undissolved and after some time settles down at the bottom of solution.

The process of filtration is used to separate sand from the above solution. It can be performed with several types of filter media. Nature of the precipitate and other factors dictate which filter medium must be used. The most convenient ways of filtration are either through a filter paper or through a filter crucible.
